questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Inner Product of Two Complex Vectors
questions.problem:
Given that $x,y\in {C}^{3},$ compute the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨x,y⟩$ of the following two vectors.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}i \\ 2i \\ -i\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}1+3i \\ -i \\ -i\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the definition of the standard Hermitian inner product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & ={x}_{1}\overset{―}{{y}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\overset{―}{{y}_{2}}+{x}_{3}\overset{―}{{y}_{3}} \\  & =i\cdot (\overset{―}{1+3i})+(2i)\cdot (\overset{―}{-i})+(-i)\cdot (\overset{―}{-i}) \\  & =i\cdot (1-3i)+2i\cdot i+(-i)\cdot \text{i} \\  & =(3+i)+(-2)+1 \\  & =2+i.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨a,b⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $i⟨a,b⟩=⟨a,-ib⟩$ for any  $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- There is vector $a\in {C}^{n}$ such that  $⟨a,a⟩<0$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. A complex number is equal to its conjugate if and only if it is a real number. The inner product over $C$  is a complex number in general.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,-ib⟩=\overset{―}{(-i)}⟨a,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false.  The inner product over $C$ is positive-definite. So, for any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have
$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩\ge 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨ia,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=⟨\alpha a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$
- $⟨ia,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true.  Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out.

- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument and linearity in the first argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\overset{―}{(\overset{―}{\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩=⟨\alpha a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that $⟨a,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}.$ Therefore, if $a\ne 0,$ then

$$
⟨ia,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\notin R.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨2a+3b,\,c⟩$ if 

$\,$ $⟨c,a⟩=2-\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨b,c⟩=1+2\text{i}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is linear in the first argument: 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2a+3b,\,c⟩ & =⟨2a,c⟩+⟨3b,c⟩ \\  & =2⟨a,c⟩+3⟨b,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2⟨a,c⟩+3⟨b,c⟩ & =2\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}+3⟨b,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨c,a⟩$ and $⟨b,c⟩:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}+3⟨b,c⟩ & =2(\overset{―}{2-\text{i}})+3(1+2\text{i}) \\  & =2(2+\text{i})+3(1+2\text{i}) \\  & =4+2\text{i}+3+6\text{i} \\  & =7+8\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

  $⟨a,b⟩=3-2\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨c,a⟩=2+\text{i}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is linear in the first argument: 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\text{i}a,\,b+c⟩ & =⟨\text{i}a,b⟩+⟨\text{i}a,c⟩ \\  & =\text{i}⟨a,b⟩+\text{i}⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

  

Next, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{i}⟨a,b⟩+\text{i}⟨a,c⟩ & =\text{i}⟨a,b⟩+\text{i}\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨a,b⟩$ and $⟨c,a⟩:$    

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{i}⟨a,b⟩+\text{i}\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩} & =\text{i}(3-2\text{i})+\text{i}\overset{―}{(2+\text{i})} \\  & =\text{i}(3-2\text{i})+\text{i}(2-\text{i}) \\  & =2+3\text{i}+1+2\text{i} \\  & =3+5\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is linear in the first argument: 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2a-b,\,c⟩ & =⟨2a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩ \\  & =2⟨a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2⟨a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩ & =2⟨a,c⟩-\overset{―}{⟨c,b}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨a,c⟩$ and $⟨c,b⟩:$    

$$
\begin{aligned}2⟨a,c⟩-\overset{―}{⟨c,b}⟩ & =2(8+\text{i})-(\overset{―}{4-5\text{i}}) \\  & =2(8+\text{i})-(4+5\text{i}) \\  & =16+2\text{i}-4-5\text{i} \\  & =12-3\text{i}\end{aligned}

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is linear in the first argument: 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨4a-b,\,c⟩ & =⟨4a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩ \\  & =4⟨a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry: 

$$
\begin{aligned}4⟨a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩ & =4\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}-⟨b,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨c,a⟩$ and $⟨b,c⟩:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}-⟨b,c⟩ & =4\overset{―}{(1-2\text{i})}-(2+3\text{i}) \\  & =4(1+2\text{i})-(2+3\text{i}) \\  & =4+8\text{i}-2-3\text{i} \\  & =2+5\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Properties of the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,2b+(3-2\text{i})c⟩$ if 

$\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=1-\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨a,c⟩=3\text{i}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,\,2b+(3-2\text{i})c⟩ & =⟨a,2b⟩+⟨a,(3-2\text{i})c⟩ \\  & =\overset{―}{2}⟨a,b⟩+(\overset{―}{3-2\text{i}})⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =2⟨a,b⟩+(3+2\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}2⟨a,b⟩+(3+2\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =2\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+(3+2\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+(3+2\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =2\cdot \overset{―}{1-\text{i}}+(3+2\text{i})\cdot (3\text{i}) \\  & =2\cdot (1+\text{i})-6+9\text{i} \\  & =-4+11\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Inner Product of Two Complex Vectors
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $\mathbf x, \mathbf y\in\mathbb C^3,$ compute the standard Hermitian inner product $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle$ of the following two vectors.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14057166/assets/5d0567f732027d096d674c2513a41a9c32b87c78bb0203d60653d555c8c9a3b9.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the definition of the standard Hermitian inner product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & ={x}_{1}\overset{―}{{y}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\overset{―}{{y}_{2}}+{x}_{3}\overset{―}{{y}_{3}} \\  & =i\cdot (\overset{―}{-3})+(-2)\cdot \overset{―}{4+i}+0\cdot \overset{―}{5} \\  & =i\cdot (-3)+(-2)\cdot (4-i)+0 \\  & =-3i-8+2i \\  & =-8-i.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ over $\mathbb{C}.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle\in\mathbb R$ for any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n$

- $\langle \mathrm{i}\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle =  \langle \mathbf{a},  -\mathrm{i} \mathbf{b} \rangle$ for any  $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n$

- $\langle\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a},\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number for any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number, and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. The inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ is a complex number in general.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the linearity in the first argument  and the antilinearity in the second argument, we have

$$
\langle  \mathrm{i}\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle =  \mathrm{i}\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle  = \langle \mathbf{a}, \overline{\, \mathrm{i}\, } \mathbf{b} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a},- \mathrm{i} \mathbf{b} \rangle
$$

 
for any  $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, by the linearity in the first argument  and the antilinearity in the second argument, we have

$$
\langle\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a},\mathrm{i} \mathbf{a} \rangle =\mathrm{i}\cdot \bar{ \mathrm{i} }\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = -\mathrm{i}^2\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle= \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle
$$

 
for any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n.$ But by positive-definiteness, this is a nonnegative real number.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying Properties of the Hermitian Inner Product
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $\langle \,\cdot\,, \,\cdot\, \rangle$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $\mathbb{C},$ find $\big\langle -2\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}, \: \mathbf{c} \big\rangle$ if 

$$
\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = 3+5\text{i}, \quad \quad \langle \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = 2-4\text{i}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \alpha \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \alpha \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C},$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle \quad$ and $\quad \langle \mathbf{a}, \alpha\mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\alpha} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $\mathbf{a}\in \mathbb{C}^n,$ we have

$\qquad$ $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle$ is a non-negative real number, and $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ is linear in the first argument: 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-2a+3b,\,c⟩ & =⟨-2a,c⟩+⟨3b,c⟩ \\  & =-2⟨a,c⟩+3⟨b,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the fact that the inner product over $\mathbb{C}$ has conjugate symmetry: 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2⟨a,c⟩+3⟨b,c⟩ & =-2⟨a,c⟩+3\overset{―}{⟨c,b⟩}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c} \rangle$ and $\langle \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{b} \rangle \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2⟨a,c⟩+3\overset{―}{⟨c,b⟩} & =-2(3+5\text{i})+3\overset{―}{(2-4\text{i})} \\  & =-2(3+5\text{i})+3(2+4\text{i}) \\  & =-6-10\text{i}+6+12\text{i} \\  & =2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$
